plain_text: Bacteria already have potassium channels, the same kind of pore that brings a neuron back to rest after it fires.
note: Present in all three domains of life.

plain_text: The receptors that let brain cells hear glutamate and GABA, the main 'go' and 'stop' signals, have relatives in bacteria and plants.
source: Chen et al. (1999) Nature 402:817; Tasneem et al. (2005) Genome Biol. 6:R4; Lam et al. (1998) Nature 396:125

first_living_group: Choanoflagellates and other single-celled relatives of animals
plain_text: Single-celled relatives of animals fire calcium spikes through voltage-gated channels, the trigger that later releases signals at every synapse.
The channel that makes the fast nerve spike first appears in the single-celled relatives of animals. Its sodium-only version evolved later, separately in jellyfish and in bilaterians.
source: Liebeskind, Hillis & Zakon (2011) PNAS 108:9154; Gur Barzilai et al. (2012) Cell Rep. 2:242

plain_text: The proteins that fuse a packet of signal with the cell membrane, the core of a synapse's 'send' side, are already in choanoflagellates.

first_living_group: Common ancestor of placozoans, jellyfish and bilaterians
plain_text: Opsins, the light-catching proteins of every animal eye, arose before the split between jellyfish and animals with a head.
Sponges have no neurons, yet their cells hold most of the proteins that build the receiving side of a synapse.
source: Sakarya et al. (2007) PLoS ONE 2:e506; Alié & Manuel (2010) BMC Evol. Biol. 10:34
note: Dated by the sponge fossil marker; the genes are older than that.

plain_text: Trichoplax, an animal with no neurons, uses small peptides much like neuropeptides to switch between gliding, turning and feeding.
source: Senatore, Reese & Smith (2017) PNAS 114:E6378; Varoqueaux et al. (2018) Curr. Biol. 28:3495

plain_text: Gap junctions let current pass straight from one cell to the next, the fastest kind of synapse. Animals with nerves use innexins; vertebrates later invented connexins.

plain_title: A second way to build nerves
plain_text: Comb jellies lack many standard neurotransmitter genes, and their nerve net is fused into one continuous cell. Their nerves may have evolved separately.
source: Moroz et al. (2014) Nature 510:109; Burkhardt et al. (2023) Science 380:293
note: Whether comb jellies evolved nerves on their own is still debated.

plain_text: Proteins that wrap nerve fibres in myelin appear with jawed fish. Jawless lampreys have none.
note: Dated from fossil placoderm skulls whose nerve openings imply myelinated nerves.
